topic.description: EEG signal processing, sleep staging, neural time series, modeling, and practical analysis methods.

papers.title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models.
papers.abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.

papers.title: Isoflurane anesthesia CNS recovery state: ultra-slow oscillations and cellular-stress-responsive gene expression.
papers.abstract: General anesthesia and NREM sleep share slow-wave EEG features, yet whether anesthesia substitutes for physiological sleep remains unclear. We compared recovery from 4h of isoflurane anesthesia (IA) with time-matched sleep and sleep deprivation (SD) in male C57BL/6J mice using continuous EEG/EMG recordings and frontal cortex RNA sequencing. IA recovery produced transient, rebound arousal, reduced early NREM and REM sleep, and, fragmented subsequent NREM bouts, and persistant, ultra-slow EEG-oscillations that normalized within two weeks. Whereas, SD induced consolidated rebound sleep and slow wave activity. Transcriptomic profiling at ZT6 showed that IA and SD induced largely distinct cortical gene-expression programs. IA preferentially enriched integrated stress response and unfolded protein response genes, whereas SD showed a comparatively orthogonal, growth-permissive, mTOR-associated profile. Although IA-induced gene-expression suggests cellular stress, corticosterone measurements argued against systemic stress as the primary driver. These findings indicate that isoflurane recovery is neurophysiologically and molecularly distinct from restorative sleep.

papers.title: EEG-SDL-Net: biomedical EEG signal classification via multi-level supervised Kolmogorov-Arnold networks.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel supervised deep learning framework for EEG signal classification based on hierarchical one-dimensional convolutional neural networks with Sobel-based temporal enhancement, channel attention, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), and multi-level deep supervision. The proposed framework is designed to improve feature representation, robustness to EEG variability, and computational efficiency for Edge AI deployment. The proposed architecture addresses the challenges of EEG signal variability, nonlinear temporal dynamics, and robust feature extraction. The framework integrates a 1D Sobel projection module for local temporal feature enhancement, a channel-wise attention mechanism for adaptive electrode selection, and KAN to capture complex non-linear relationships. Furthermore, a deep supervision strategy is employed to stabilize training and ensure robust gradient flow. Experimental evaluations on the SEED-VIG dataset demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Performance benchmarks on edge devices, such as the Raspberry Pi 4, show a real-time inference latency of 15 ms, confirming the framework's suitability for Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) and portable monitoring systems. The complete source code has been made openly available and permanently archived through Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21441822.

papers.title: Discrete cortico-hippocampal circuit states underlie mood state transitions in depression.
papers.abstract: The hippocampus has long been implicated in depression, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Leveraging precision functional mapping in densely sampled individuals and large cross-sectional cohorts, and validating key results in direct intracranial EEG recordings from the human brain, we show that hippocampal connectivity alternates between two discrete and opposing network states on the order of minutes: one dominated by default mode network (DMN) coupling and another by sensorimotor system (SM) coupling. This dynamic switching is a fundamental property of hippocampal function in both healthy brains and in major depressive disorder (MDD). In MDD, this equilibrium is disrupted, such that the DMN-dominant state is overrepresented. In densely sampled individuals, hippocampus-DMN coupling tracks symptom fluctuations over time and normalizes after electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), which drives switches in hippocampal connectivity away from the DMN-dominant state and toward the SM-dominant state-an effect that was closely linked to a positive treatment response. Direct intracranial recordings in patients with MDD identified analogous fluctuations in hippocampal-DMN theta synchrony, which tracks symptom fluctuations over hours and days. Together, these findings identify a dynamic cortico-hippocampal mechanism underlying depression and indicate that successful neuromodulation treatments such as ECT act in part by restoring a dynamic equilibrium in hippocampal network connectivity.

papers.title: Alpha-range neural oscillations are associated with multiple dynamic brain networks.
papers.abstract: We asked whether alpha range (8-12 Hz) EEG neural oscillations, a robust indicator of cortical excitability, are associated with dynamic BOLD brain networks. Two independent EEG-fMRI resting-state datasets (discovery: n = 94 and replication: n = 33) show that low-and high-alpha periods are associated with dynamic BOLD coactivation patterns (dCAPS) involving multiple dynamic networks rather than a single static network. Unique BOLD dCAPs consisting of visual cortex activation along with sensorimotor and attention networks in addition to the posterior thalamus, were mainly associated with periods of low-alpha power. However, overlapping BOLD dCAPs consisting of default, control, and attention networks were associated with periods of both low-and high-alpha power. The results suggest low-alpha dCAPS contain unique temporal-dependent configurations related to visual, sensorimotor, and attention networks while both low-and high-alpha dCAPs consist of overlapping temporal-dependent configurations involving CON, DMN, and attention networks involved in internal and external cognition. These findings reconcile discrepancies across static connectivity EEG-fMRI findings by showing that distinct transient BOLD configurations are associated with similar patterns of alpha EEG modulation in visual cortex, providing a dynamic framework for the gating function of alpha oscillations.

papers.title: Coupled neuro-fluid dynamics in human bioelectromagnetism.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) are widely interpreted as direct, non-invasive measures of neural population activity, assuming surrounding tissue and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) act as passive volume conductors that distorts but do not contribute to signal generation. Using conductive-fluid phantom experiments, structural magnetic resonance imaging, and in vivo EEG and MEG recordings, the present report challenges this assumption. Mechanically driven conductive fluid generated structured, oscillatory, source-localizable electromagnetic signals resembling M/EEG in the absence of neural tissue, and interindividual differences in CSF volume systematically moderated M/EEG signal amplitude. These findings suggest that, at the scales accessed by invasive and non-invasive electrophysiology, electromagnetic and mechanical processes form a coupled system in which contributions of neural currents and fluid motion cannot readily be uniquely separated.

papers.title: Cortical physiological arousal following termination of absence seizures.
papers.abstract: Although the brain state preceding and during absence seizures has been well-characterized, the postictal brain state remains largely unexplored due to the prevailing assumption that absence seizures have minimal or no postictal changes. To address this gap, scalp EEG recordings from 55 patients with 3-4 Hz spike-wave discharges across four multi-site cohorts were analyzed. Spectral power was measured relative to each seizure's preictal baseline, and the postictal period was compared to a time-matched preictal window. Rather than an immediate return to baseline after seizure offset, a significant broadband increase in EEG power was observed in the gamma (>25 Hz) and delta (<4 Hz) frequency bands, followed by a gradual decline over the next 15 s to 30 s. In contrast, no comparable change preceded the seizures. This suggests that recovery from an absence seizure is an active process with a characteristic electrophysiological signature consistent with cortical activation and arousal. Thus, postictal arousal may facilitate exit from the seizure state, and with further work could serve as an electrophysiological marker and therapeutic target for recovery in absence epilepsy.

papers.title: Two-stage spatiotemporal graph neural network framework for seizure onset zone localization.
papers.abstract: Accurate localization of the seizure onset zone (SOZ) is critical for the presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy. Intracranial electroencephalography captures high-resolution seizure dynamics, but interpreting complex spatiotemporal patterns across implanted electrodes is clinically challenging. We propose a two-stage, uncertainty-aware framework for SOZ localization that integrates patient-specific seizure modeling with cross-patient probabilistic ranking to estimate the likelihood of each electrode belonging to the SOZ. The framework was evaluated on a bi-institutional cohort of 36 patients (20 with good surgical outcome, 16 with poor surgical outcome), comprising 184 seizures. In the first stage, a patient-specific spatiotemporal graph neural network modeled seizure onset as a network-level transition using directed functional connectivity graphs derived from burst-integrated electrophysiological features. Trained solely to detect preictal-to-ictal transitions, this model generated electrode probability trajectories without SOZ supervision. In the second stage, these trajectories were summarized into interpretable descriptors and used to train a patient-agnostic classifier assigning SOZ likelihood scores to electrodes. Evaluation and hyperparameter optimization were performed using nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation restricted to good outcome patients, ensuring strict patient-level separation between training, validation, and test data. Seizure onset detection was stable across patients, with comparable binary cross-entropy values between outcome groups (median = .495 vs. .438, p = .108). In good outcome patients, SOZ electrodes were prioritized among top-ranked contacts (area under the curve = .86 ± .06), with all patients exhibiting at least one SOZ electrode within the top positions. In poor outcome patients, predictions exhibited reduced spatial separability, lower likelihood magnitudes, and near-zero confidence gaps, reflecting attenuated model confidence. This two-stage framework integrates spatial interactions, temporal dynamics, and probabilistic ranking within a pipeline. By providing graded SOZ likelihood estimates and uncertainty-aware prioritization, the approach is a decision-support tool to assist hypothesis refinement during presurgical evaluation rather than as a standalone diagnostic system.

papers.title: Altered EEG-derived co-fluctuation structure in disorders of consciousness.
papers.abstract: EEG-derived functional connectivity (FC) enables high-temporal-resolution probing of neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DOC). Unlike stationary conventional FC, dynamic FC (dFC) captures fast transient neural coupling. Recent fMRI studies introduced a co‑fluctuation framework to track moment‑to‑moment connectivity change, yet whether such co-fluctuation features can quantify consciousness status remains elusive. Here, we adapt this established co-fluctuation paradigm to resting-state EEG to characterize the temporal architectures of EEG-derived FC across varying conscious states. We decomposed the co-fluctuation time series into high-amplitude frames (HAF) and low-amplitude frames (LAF), comparing their dynamics between real brain data and null models. We then analyzed co-fluctuation activities across consciousness levels at both global and local spatial scales, examining spatial variability in these patterns. By integrating HAF and LAF parameters, we evaluated their diagnostic potential for distinguishing DOC states. Results revealed reduced stability of co-fluctuations with loss of consciousness, accompanied by a shift toward random system dynamics. DOC patients exhibited reduced spatial and temporal heterogeneity in co-fluctuation activities compared to healthy controls. Both high- and low-amplitude patterns provided useful metrics for detecting consciousness levels. These findings offer novel insights into the dynamic organization of brain networks in DOC, emphasizing the significance of co-fluctuation dynamics in characterizing brain states and suggesting potential biomarkers for assessing consciousness levels. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10580-7.

Loss of consciousness was associated with reduced co-fluctuation stability, a shift toward random system dynamics, and reduced spatial and temporal heterogeneity, with combined HAF/LAF parameters showing diagnostic potential for distinguishing DOC states.

papers.title: Faster peak alpha frequency precedes higher menstrual pain in adolescence.
papers.abstract: Brain differences in chronic pain are almost always measured after years of pain experience, leaving unresolved whether they create vulnerability to pain or result from it. Uniquely, menstrual pain has a developmentally scheduled onset (menarche, the first menstrual period), allowing the brain to be characterized before and after pain exposure occurs. Here we used longitudinal 64-channel EEG to measure resting brain activity in adolescents once before (n=250) and twice after (n=161, n=140) menarche. Before their first period, adolescents who later reported higher menstrual pain (30 or greater on a 0 to 100 VAS) already showed faster occipital peak alpha frequency compared to those who reported lower menstrual pain, a difference that persisted in the early (3 to 14 months) post-menarche time period. In contrast, oscillatory power and functional connectivity did not differ by menstrual pain group, suggesting that the widespread functional brain alterations reported in adults with painful periods take years to emerge. Peak alpha frequency increased, and theta power and connectivity decreased across the menarchal transition, consistent with typical adolescent maturation. However, longitudinal analyses stratified by higher and lower menstrual pain group suggested group specific timings for these neurodevelopmental changes. Overall, these findings suggest that early menstrual pain is not associated with widespread alterations in neural oscillations, but aspects of menstrual pain susceptibility may be reflected in resting peak alpha frequency. To our knowledge, this is the first neurophysiological trait shown to precede the onset of menstrual pain.

papers.title: Understanding Performance Plateaus and Representation Collapse in 3D MRI Transformers Trained to Classify Brain Disease.
papers.abstract: In medical imaging AI, we commonly assume that diagnostic classifiers will increase in accuracy if they are trained on more data, but in reality, their performance often plateaus. To understand this behavior, we ran a spectral analysis of 3D vision transformers, a common supervised deep learning model that can be trained to classify disease based on 3D brain MRI. For simpler classification methods such as linear discriminant analysis, the classifier performance AUC(N), when trained on a sample of size N, is known to depend on the encoder's eigenspectrum. Each class-discriminative direction in the latent space contributes only after the sample size N reaches a threshold N i = λ i /α i 2 - so the spectrum influences how performance scales with training data. Building on this theory, we show that supervised transformers compress almost all of their discriminative signal into one principal component (EVR@1 = 0.90-0.96): after this "representation collapse" happens, no further directions cross the threshold as training data increases, and accuracy plateaus. In principle, this plateau in performance could be due to either the encoder's learned feature space or the difficulty of the task. To distinguish these cases, we trained three types of supervised 3D transformers (ViT3D, MINiT, NIT) and, as a non-collapsing alternative, a frozen self-supervised encoder (DINO), to classify people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) versus cognitively normal (CN) individuals from 3D brain MRI, using data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). We froze each encoder and applied it to a new task, so that only the task difficulty varied. An "easy" task encoder (Dementia vs CN), transferred to the harder task (MCI vs CN), did not reproduce the plateau (MINiT threshold 9.2), but full retraining did (2758.5). The plateau is therefore due to the learned encoder, rather than task difficulty. Ranking the feature directions by the proportion of the disease signal they contain, we were able to identify a sign of representation collapse, i.e., a single dominant spike in the latent feature eigenspectrum. This spike was 11-26 times larger than predicted from the rest of the spectrum for the disease-trained (supervised) encoders, but was absent for DINO (0.66). To predict how transformer accuracy scales with the number of training scans, a large spike in the encoder spectrum suggests that the representation has collapsed and additional scans will not help; a small spike means that the signal is spread across many encoder latent space directions, and more training data should boost the classifier performance.

papers.title: Probing the neural geometry of conscious object perception in time.
papers.abstract: Conscious object recognition is a critical brain function, key to making sense of the plethora of visual inputs and guiding adaptive behavior. Yet, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious object recognition remains unclear. Existing proposals alternatively suggest that conscious object recognition proceeds in a "coarse-to-fine" sequence or a "fine-to-coarse" sequence. Here, we recorded high-density EEG while participants of both sexes performed a threshold-level object recognition task under different viewing conditions. Both superordinate and basic-level category information emerged early in neural activity, followed by a late superordinate category representation in an abstract format that is disentangled from low-level object features. Strikingly, in the early period, while basic-level category information positively correlated with perceptual awareness, superordinate category information negatively predicted perceptual awareness. By contrast, both superordinate and basic-level category information positively correlated with objective categorization accuracy in the early period. In the late period, both levels of category information positively correlated with awareness. These results suggest that neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate category level. Despite significant interests, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious perception remains unclear. Here, we investigated the unfolding of neural events in time that support perceptual awareness of visual objects. Using a threshold-level object perception task involving three image conditions (normal, low-pass filtered, masked) and high-density EEG, we reveal that basic and superordinate category information both emerge early in the neural activity (at ∼100 ms), but only the basic-level category representation positively contributes to awareness. By contrast, the early superordinate category representation negatively correlates with perceptual awareness. At ∼300 ms, an abstract superordinate category representation emerges, which also positively correlates with perceptual awareness. Therefore, category-level neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate level.

papers.title: Altered interictal alpha-band organization in childhood absence epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Interictal background EEG in childhood absence epilepsy (CAE) may appear normal. We asked whether drug-naive children with CAE differ from controls in alpha frequency and the regional distribution of phase-lagged synchronization, and how these differences depend on participant-specific surrogate baselines and analysis frequency. We analyzed eyes-closed resting EEG (19 channels, 26 s) from 49 drug-naive children with CAE and 83 controls. Individual alpha frequency (IAF) was estimated by spectral parameterization of posterior channels. Weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) at 12 Hz was summarized globally and as the frontal-posterior log-ratio λFP = ln(wPLIF/wPLIP), where F and P denote frontal and posterior within-region means. Participant-specific baselines were obtained from 100 circular-shift surrogates, preserving each channel's wavelet-coefficient sequence up to circular translation while altering inter-channel alignment. Group comparisons used studentized permutation tests. The regional contrast was also evaluated at each participant's IAF. IAF was lower in patients (8.80 versus 9.42 Hz; p = 0.002). At 12 Hz, controls showed posterior predominance of synchronization (λFP = -0.352), which was largely removed by circular shifting (-0.036), whereas patients' mean regional balance was near zero. After baseline subtraction, the patient-minus-control difference in λFP was 0.332 (95 % CI [0.181, 0.483]; p < 0.001; Hedges' g = 0.79). In the 131 participants with identifiable IAF, the contrast was 0.316 at 12 Hz and 0.124 at IAF (p = 0.139). A direct comparison using within-participant changes supported a larger contrast at 12 Hz (difference 0.192, 95 % CI [0.017, 0.367]; exploratory, unadjusted p = 0.032). The global wPLI difference after baseline subtraction remained uncertain (-0.021, 95 % CI [-0.044, 0.001]; p = 0.069). Drug-naive CAE was associated with slower alpha activity and reduced posterior predominance of phase-lagged synchronization at 12 Hz. Circular shifting largely removed the controls' posterior predominance, supporting a difference in regional organization sensitive to inter-channel alignment. The smaller contrast at IAF indicates that analysis frequency materially affects this finding, without establishing that alpha slowing alone explains it.

papers.title: Sleep as a vulnerability marker in clinical high-risk populations. a multimodal systematic review.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are increasingly recognized as clinically significant features of the psychosis risk state, yet no comprehensive synthesis has examined sleep across all assessment modalities in clinical high-risk (CHR) populations. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, five major databases were searched (January 1995-March 2026) for original studies assessing sleep in CHR populations, with CHR status operationalized through validated instruments. From 5218 citations, 26 studies were included. Sleep disturbances affected 59-80% of CHR individuals. Actigraphy predicted positive symptom worsening at 12-month follow-up. Experience sampling identified nocturnal awakenings as predictors of next-day paranoia and derealization, mediated by morning negative affect. Sleep disturbance predicted symptom severity over time, accelerated transition among converters, and was independently associated with suicidal ideation. High-density EEG polysomnography documented reduced prefrontal spindle duration, elevated non-rapid eye movement (NREM) gamma power, and reduced slow wave density - replicated across independent cohorts. A multimodal neuroimaging study identified whole-thalamus-dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) hypoconnectivity as a convergent thalamocortical marker. Sleep disturbances in CHR populations span multiple neurobiologically distinct domains. Polysomnographic markers - spindle parameters and NREM gamma power - represent the most neurophysiologically specific signatures identified. Standardized sleep assessment should be integrated into CHR clinical protocols as both a prognostic tool and a modifiable therapeutic target.

papers.title: Depressive status modulates hippocampal-cortical dynamics during acute nicotine use.
papers.abstract: Nicotine use disorder shows heterogeneity in treatment response, potentially reflecting differences in underlying neural circuitry, particularly in the presence of depression. We examined real-time neural dynamics during nicotine inhalation in two chronic users - one with depression and one without - using simultaneous hippocampal recordings from responsive neurostimulation (RNS) electrodes and scalp EEG. Oscillatory activity and hippocampal-cortical connectivity were analyzed in relation to mood and craving. Oscillatory activity tracked mood in the non-depressed individual but was attenuated or reversed in the depressed individual, suggesting reduced reward-related neural responsiveness. In contrast, both participants showed reduced alpha hippocampal-cortical connectivity following nicotine use, suggesting a shift from reward-seeking to reward and relief processing. These findings support a network-based framework of nicotine-driven neural dynamics and provide preliminary evidence that depressive status may modulate these processes. Although limited to two cases, this work highlights the potential for identifying neurophysiological subtypes of nicotine users and informs future efforts toward personalized treatment approaches.

papers.title: Aging Is Associated with Reduced Topographic Differentiation Between Speaking and Silent Reading.
papers.abstract: Aging affects how neural activity is organized and specialized, but its impact on neural differentiation across language tasks remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether aging influences neural differentiation during speaking and silent reading. Fifteen young adults and 15 older adults completed speaking and silent-reading tasks in a delayed-response paradigm while we collected electroencephalography (EEG) data. We examined EEG signal strength using time-resolved global field power (GFP), spatial configuration using topographic analysis of variance (TANOVA), and task-specific neural differentiation using the global dissimilarity index (DISS). We also examined the relationship between neural and behavioral measures, including digit-span scores and speech onset time. We found that speaking was associated with higher GFP than silent reading in the 388-800 ms interval, with no significant effects of group or group × task interaction, indicating similar EEG strength across groups. TANOVA revealed age-related differences in scalp topography in the 229-334 ms and 377-538 ms intervals, a task effect in the 618-723 ms interval, and a group × task interaction in the 562-636 ms interval. Notably, young adults had greater DISS than older adults during the 508-629 ms and 660-800 ms intervals, reflecting more distinct neural configurations for speaking and reading. We did not find significant correlations between DISS or GFP and behavioral measures, and the two groups performed similarly on behavioral measures. Overall, aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between speaking and silent reading, especially during later processing stages (e.g., motor command preparation), while preserving overall EEG activity and behavioral performance. These findings may suggest that aging reduces neural network specificity (as previously suggested) and alters spatial organization without necessarily impairing behavior.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-generated and algorithmically personalized music interventions and their effects on brain function, behavior, and health: a critical review.
papers.abstract: This critical review synthesizes empirical studies of algorithmically personalized and artificial-intelligence-generated music interventions reporting neurophysiological, neuroimaging, or objective behavioral outcomes. Literature was identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library through 12 August 2026, with CNKI and Wanfang searched on 22 September 2026, supplemented by citation tracking. Twenty-one eligible studies (at least 1,005 participants) were identified. Five things the term artificial intelligence covers in this literature are separated: algorithmic selection from a corpus, rule-based sonification, parametric modulation of pre-existing material, machine-learning generative composition, and closed-loop delivery contingent on the listener's own signal. Only three studies used a machine-learning generative model, so most of the evidence concerns algorithmic personalization of existing material. Studies of closed-loop neural systems reported the most consistent neurophysiological signal, and music-based alpha neurofeedback produced higher normalized alpha power than yoked random feedback. In an open-loop design, personalized EEG-derived music was reported to attenuate anxiety induction where self-selected preferred music and silence did not, with enhanced prefrontal theta oscillations as the associated correlate. Eight studies carried a comparator capable of isolating an algorithmic component from music exposure, and all eight favored the algorithmic condition. These eight address different causal questions, use different designs, and point to no single mechanism, so their results are best read as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Evidence quality was very low throughout. The median reported sample size was 22, no study blinded participants or measured expectancy, and no specific finding has been independently replicated. GRADE certainty was very low for every outcome domain, covering EEG oscillatory power, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, epileptiform activity, and cognitive, behavioral and affective outcomes. Neurophysiological change is reported more often than behavioral change, and behavioral change more often than clinical benefit. The evidence supports continued investigation and does not support clinical deployment. Eight reporting and design requirements for future trials are proposed.

All eight comparator studies favored the algorithmic condition, but designs were heterogeneous and no finding was independently replicated, so the evidence supports further investigation rather than clinical deployment.

papers.title: Ion Channels and Morphology Drive Widespread Resonance in Human Cortical Interneurons.
papers.abstract: Cortical neurons respond preferentially to specific network oscillation frequencies-a phenomenon driven by membrane potential resonance. While well studied in human pyramidal neurons, adult human interneuron resonance remains largely unexplored. Using Patch-seq, acute electrophysiology, organotypic cultures, and computational modeling, we investigated the mechanisms underlying resonance across human LAMP5, VIP, PV, and SST interneurons. Resonance is significantly more prevalent in human versus mouse interneurons, peaking in parvalbumin (PV) cells. Unlike human pyramidal neurons, interneuron resonance is independent of cortical depth. Instead, resonance frequency and strength strongly correlate with low input resistance, prominent membrane voltage sag, and enriched expression of HCN1, KCNJ16, and CACNA1A ion channel genes. HCN blockade abolished resonance, while enhanced HCN-mediated sag increased resonance prevalence and strength. Finally, computational models revealed that human morphological features and ion channels sharpen frequency tuning, translating into distinct suprathreshold output under noisy, in vivo-like conditions. These findings reveal fundamental species differences governing human cortical microcircuit dynamics.

HCN blockade abolished resonance, and models showed human morphology and ion channels sharpen frequency tuning under in vivo-like noisy conditions.

papers.title: Self-Guided Beta-Responsive Visual Neurofeedback in a Public Exhibition: Feasibility and Usability Randomized Controlled rial.
papers.abstract: Neurofeedback is studied for stress and anxiety regulation, but most systems require supervision or research-grade equipment. Consumer electroencephalography (EEG) could broaden access, yet autonomous first-contact feasibility, usability, and baseline neural-state effects remain unclear. We assessed autonomous completion and usability, tested whether a fixed breathing pacer improved outcomes over visual neurofeedback alone, and explored whether pretask resting beta was associated with usability. We conducted a single-session, 2-arm randomized feasibility and usability trial at a public science exhibition in Bern, Switzerland, between March and June 2025. Eligible adults were aged 18 years or older, could read German or French, and reported no epilepsy or implanted electronic device. A tablet app guided participants without experimenter assistance through consent, setup, a 30-second eyes-closed baseline, 1:1 randomization, a 120-second beta-responsive task, and questionnaires. The final analytic sample included participants assigned to visual neurofeedback only (VN; n=27) or visual neurofeedback plus a 6 breaths/minute breathing pacer (VN+BP; n=25). Outcomes were usability, relaxation, and state mindfulness. Data were collected prospectively; no secondary data were used. Analyses used Mann-Whitney U, chi-square, Spearman, and permutation tests (2-sided, α=.05); EEG outcome and item analyses were exploratory. Of 110 visitors initiating a session, 79 completed the task with a valid EEG recording (71.8%, 95% CI 62.8-79.4) and 52 met analytic criteria (47.3%, 95% CI 38.2%-56.5%). Participants (35 women) had a mean age of 39.0 (SD 11.3) years. Usability was good (System Usability Scale [SUS] mean 72.3, SD 14.7; 95% CI 68.3-76.2), and 31/52 participants scored at least 68 (59.6%, 95% CI 46.1%-71.8%). Usability did not differ between VN and VN+BP (median 75.0, IQR 62.5-81.3 vs median 72.5, IQR 65.0-90.0; Mann-Whitney U=362.5, P=.65; rank-biserial r=-0.07, 95% CI -0.39 to 0.25). Relaxation (median 63.0, IQR 50.0-80.0 vs median 61.0, IQR 50.0-67.0; Mann-Whitney U=276.5, P=.27; r=0.18, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.49) and mindfulness (median 2.4, IQR 2.1-2.8 vs median 2.5, IQR 2.0-3.2; Mann-Whitney U=346.5, P=.68; r=-0.07, 95% CI -0.39 to 0.26) did not differ. Higher resting beta was associated with lower SUS before correction (Spearman ρ=-0.31, 95% CI -0.54 to -0.04; raw P=.03), but not after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (adjusted P=.30). SUS item analyses showed a global pattern (permutation P=.02), strongest for functional integration (ρ=-0.43, 95% CI -0.63 to -0.18; Holm-adjusted P=.01). This trial evaluated an autonomous consumer-EEG neurofeedback system integrating self-fitting, signal-quality checking, baseline calibration, adaptive feedback, randomization, and self-report without operator support. Many first-time users completed the autonomous workflow with acceptable-to-good usability; a fixed, open-loop breathing pacer did not improve usability, relaxation, or state mindfulness; and higher resting beta showed a preliminary association with lower perceived usability. These findings support autonomous consumer-EEG neurofeedback and motivate work on adaptive onboarding, validated EEG pipelines, and objective self-regulation outcomes.

papers.title: Social Media Use and Emotional Reactivity to Negative Stimuli: An ERP Investigation.
papers.abstract: Exposure to violent media has long been associated with reduced emotional reactivity, empathy, and moral sensitivity, which is a phenomenon commonly referred to as emotional desensitization. Although numerous studies have explored this process in video games and films, its neural correlates in social media contexts remain insufficiently examined. This study aimed to examine whether individual differences in social media use are associated with neural responses to negative emotional stimuli. Fifty-six healthy young adults participated in an electroencephalography (EEG) experiment, during which they passively viewed negative, neutral, and positive images selected from the International Affective Picture System (IAPS). Emotional processing was assessed using two event-related potential (ERP) components: the Early Posterior Negativity (EPN, 200-300 ms) and the Late Positive Potential (LPP, 300-800 ms). Amplitude differences across stimulus categories and brain regions were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA. Negative images elicited significantly greater LPP amplitudes compared to neutral and positive images, particularly across central, parietal, and temporal regions, indicating sustained emotional engagement. In contrast, EPN amplitudes did not differ significantly across conditions, suggesting that early attentional mechanisms were not modulated by emotional valence. No group differences were observed between participants with high and low levels of social media use. The findings indicate that typical social media exposure was not associated with reduced neural responsiveness in this sample. Emotional engagement with negative stimuli remains intact, supporting the notion that desensitization is a gradual, context-dependent process influenced by the nature and intensity of digital exposure.

papers.title: Sensorimotor expertise effects extend from dance to face perception.
papers.abstract: Domain specific expertise affects neural and behavioral processes of perception and memory. We explore if sensorimotor expertise extends to other relevant social mechanisms, such as the neural processing of emotional faces. We recorded brain activity of 26 dancers and 26 non-dancers using visual and somatosensory evoked potentials (VEPs, SEPs) during an emotion and sex discrimination task on happy, afraid, and neutral faces. We predicted expertise-related modulation of visual facial emotion processing in visual and somatosensory areas. EEG results revealed distinct visual and somatosensory ERP patterns in the two groups. VEP findings showed that dancers distinguished between neutral and emotional faces at N170 and P200. Non-dancers differentiated between the three emotions with more lateralized processing. For SEPs, dancers uniquely showed early emotion effects (P50) in central somatosensory regions and task-modulated somatosensory engagement at later stages (N80, P100). Non-dancers showed later, localized somatosensory effects. In summary, dance expertise shapes both visual and somatosensory processing of facial emotion, indicating a broader neural representation of emotions. These findings provide novel evidence for a differential facial emotion processing in dancers, extending the dance expertise modulation beyond perception of dance-specific stimuli, to face emotion perception. Overall, this work highlights the strong influence of sensorimotor training on emotion perception.

papers.title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients.
papers.abstract: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

papers.title: Conserved Thalamic Astrocytic Pathology in Mice and Patients Links TBI to Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) can emerge months to years after traumatic brain injury (TBI) and is a major cause of morbidity, yet the pathological processes that distinguish TBI progressing to epilepsy remain poorly defined. Here, we combined longitudinal multimodal imaging, electrophysiology, neuropathology, and human imaging and postmortem analyses to identify cross-species features associated with PTE. In a mouse model of PTE-prone TBI, injury produced widespread brain pathology, whereas animals developing PTE showed disproportionate thalamic atrophy, white-matter abnormalities with reduced optic tract fractional anisotropy, and persistent metabolic alterations. Histological analyses revealed pronounced thalamic astrocytic reactivity, reduced cytoskeletal complexity, and impaired expression of proteins involved in glutamate homeostasis. Using an early ECoG signature to prospectively stratify PTE risk, we found that astrocytic simplification and accumulation of insoluble GFAP were already present during the latent period before spontaneous seizure onset. In patients with PTE, thalamic volume loss and reduced posterior thalamic radiation fractional anisotropy independently improved PTE classification beyond clinical variables. PTE patients also showed reduced pulvinar-centered thalamocortical functional connectivity involving visual and default mode networks. Postmortem tissue further demonstrated pronounced astrocytic reactivity and reduced astrocytic complexity in cortex and thalamus. In contrast, IBA1-defined microglial reactivity did not distinguish PTE from non-PTE at the chronic time points examined. Together, these findings identify a conserved thalamocortical phenotype associated with PTE and show that astrocytic remodeling emerges before spontaneous seizures. The convergence of cellular pathology with structural, metabolic, and functional abnormalities identifies the thalamus as a candidate hub of post-traumatic epileptogenesis and provides translational markers for tracking disease progression after TBI.

papers.title: Repetitive clustered low-voltage fast activity on intracranial electroencephalogram in mild malformation of cortical development with oligodendroglial hyperplasia and epilepsy: A candidate electroencephalographic biomarker study.
papers.abstract: Mild malformation of cortical development with oligodendroglial hyperplasia and epilepsy (MOGHE) is a recently recognized cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy. It is often magnetic resonance imaging-negative or radiologically resembles focal cortical dysplasias, which makes recognition difficult and limits presurgical counseling. We aimed to identify an intracranial electroencephalographic (iEEG) biomarker that distinguishes MOGHE from other developmental brain lesions encountered in epilepsy surgery. We analyzed long-term stereo-EEG and subdural recordings in a retrospective multicenter test cohort (18 MOGHE, 20 non-MOGHE) to identify an iEEG pattern distinguishing MOGHE from other developmental brain lesions. We then evaluated its diagnostic performance by blinded visual assessment in an independent single-center validation cohort (11 MOGHE, 11 non-MOGHE). Firth-penalized multivariable logistic regression tested whether MOGHE histology independently predicted the presence of this pattern after adjustment for spasms, frontal localization, age at seizure onset, and age at implantation. Finally, within MOGHE, we assessed whether resection of the territory exhibiting this pattern was associated with postsurgical seizure freedom. We identified highly stereotyped clusters of very brief low-voltage fast activity (LVFA), recurring in statuslike episodes lasting several minutes and sometimes lacking clear clinical symptoms. LVFA clusters occurred in 16 of 18 MOGHE and in no non-MOGHE patients in the test cohort. In the validation cohort, visual identification of LVFA clusters correctly classified 10 of 11 MOGHE and 10 of 11 non-MOGHE cases (overall agreement = 90.9%, 95% Wilson confidence interval = 72.2%-97.5%). MOGHE histology was the dominant independent predictor of LVFA clusters. Within MOGHE, resection of LVFA cluster territory was associated with postsurgical seizure freedom (Mann-Whitney U-test, p = .0021). Because LVFA clusters can be recognized visually on routine iEEG without specialized software, they may provide a clinically applicable candidate biomarker for presurgical identification of MOGHE and support surgical planning and outcome prediction. Prospective studies should validate their diagnostic and prognostic utility.

papers.title: Abnormal SEP recovery amongst multimodal electrophysiological studies to indicate cortical dysfunction in PME.
papers.abstract: Progressive myoclonic epilepsies (PMEs) are rare neurodegenerative disorders characterized by cortical hyperexcitability and progressive neurological deterioration. We aimed to identify electrophysiological markers of cortical dysfunction using multimodal neurophysiological assessment. Seventeen adult PME patients underwent clinical evaluation and video-EEG recording. Somatosensory evoked potentials (SEP), SEP recovery function and surround inhibition, blink reflex, and motor evoked potentials (MEP) were assessed in 11 patients and compared with 11 matched healthy controls. Generalized epileptiform discharges were observed in all patients. SEP recordings demonstrated increased N20/P25 amplitudes and prolonged P14, N18, and P25 latencies. SEP recovery showed marked attenuation at the shortest interstimulus interval followed by rapid amplitude recovery. Surround inhibition was preserved. Blink reflex studies revealed prolonged R2 latencies and increased amplitudes. MEP parameters did not differ significantly between groups. PME is associated with abnormal SEP recovery dynamics and giant SEPs, consistent with impaired somatosensory inhibitory processing. Blink reflex abnormalities suggest additional subcortical involvement, whereas corticospinal excitability appears relatively preserved.

papers.title: EEG responses to monosodium glutamate concentration and individual umami sensitivity in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: Taste perception depends on stimulus intensity and individual sensitivity, but how these factors shape cortical responses to monosodium glutamate (MSG) is unclear. We combined psychophysics and 64-channel EEG in 38 healthy adults grouped by MSG detection threshold. Increasing MSG concentration reduced fronto-central P200 and posterior N200 amplitudes (FDR-corrected p < .001; partial η2 = 0.30-0.50), and evoked beta power was highest at the lowest concentration. Exploratory source analyses showed weaker right orbitofrontal-dorsolateral prefrontal beta-band (14-30 Hz) connectivity at higher concentrations. The ERP effects were robust to alternative preprocessing. No group effect survived correction, and sensitivity could not be decoded above chance. Lower detection thresholds were associated with larger posterior late positive potentials (exploratory). EEG captures robust neural responses to MSG concentration and may complement sensory panels, whereas neural markers of individual sensitivity require larger samples.

papers.title: A Human iPSC-Derived Neuron and Glioma Culture Model Reveals Increased Neuronal Excitability and Loss of GABAergic Inhibition.
papers.abstract: Gliomas engage in bidirectional interactions with neural circuits, driving hyperexcitability, disruption of excitatory-inhibitory balance, and tumor-associated seizures. Human in vitro models that enable functional interrogation of tumor-induced changes in glutamatergic-GABAergic neuronal crosstalk remain limited. We established a defined human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived culture comprising of glutamatergic neurons, GABAergic neurons, and astrocytes with and without glioma cells. Network maturation and function were characterized using immunocytochemistry, multi-electrode array recordings, and whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology. Neuronal cultures developed mature synaptic architecture, spontaneous coordinated network activity, and suppression of neuronal firing following treatment with the GABA-A agonist muscimol, demonstrating functional GABAergic signaling. Glioma incorporation increased spike rate, increased coordinated network activity, and reversed the response to muscimol from suppression to elevation of neuronal firing, indicating disrupted GABAergic signaling. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings demonstrated increased intrinsic excitability of glutamatergic neurons following glioma co-culture, characterized by increased action potential firing frequency and increased action potential amplitude. This human iPSC-derived glutamatergic-GABAergic neuron model recapitulates key features of tumor-induced neuronal dysfunction while enabling complementary network- and single-cell analyses. The model provides a relevant, scalable, and accessible system for mechanistic investigation of bidirectional neuron-glioma interactions and preclinical evaluation of therapies targeting tumor-induced neuronal dysfunction.

papers.title: Cellularized, needle-deployed intracortical arrays for brain electrophysiology.
papers.abstract: Bioelectronic medicine enables direct interfacing with native cell populations but remains limited by poor long-term integration and minimal interaction with non-electroactive cells. In contrast, regenerative medicine promotes tissue integration yet lacks bidirectional functionality. Here, we present a hybrid implantation methodology combining a tissue engineered cellularized hydrogel with a neural recording array for simultaneous delivery into the brain via needle placement. This approach enables co-localized transplantation of cells and electronics while minimizing surgical footprint. Post-implantation electrophysiological recordings show functional integration with surrounding neural tissue, demonstrating the feasibility of this platform for coupled bioelectronic sensing and regenerative capabilities. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1557/s43579-026-01033-7.

papers.title: Large-scale all-optical electrophysiology links excitability and connectivity to circuit dynamics in vivo.
papers.abstract: To understand neural computations, one would like to relate circuit dynamics to neuronal intrinsic excitability and connectivity. We developed tools for large-scale all-optical electrophysiology and applied them to approximately 300 layer 1 interneurons per mouse in vivo . Across two mice, targeted stimulation and voltage imaging identified 1,469 inhibitory and 5,752 directed electrical connections among 14,312 tested pairs. Presynaptic identity was more strongly associated with inhibitory post-synaptic potential (IPSP) amplitude, whereas postsynaptic identity was more strongly associated with IPSP decay time. Gap junctional and synaptic interactions had distinct spatiotemporal kernels, with corresponding signatures in spontaneous activity. Excitability measured under optogenetic stimulus predicted spiking responses to subthreshold voltage, depolarization rate, and spike history during spontaneous firing. Genetic subtypes also showed different behavioral-state-dependent voltage-to-spike relationships despite similar population-average subthreshold voltages. These measurements link cellular properties and pairwise interactions to spontaneous circuit dynamics, establishing an approach for functional circuit mapping in vivo . papers.title: Voltage versus concentration in ion channels: Physical signatures reveal rate-limiting steps.
papers.abstract: Within the field of electrophysiology, I-V curves are a primary experimental means of characterizing ion channel behavior. By directly measuring ionic currents across membranes, electrophysiological techniques quantify key properties, including conductance, ion selectivity, and voltage dependence. We demonstrate a method of linking experimentally observed ion flux with microscopic mechanistic properties of channels. Although voltage and chemical potential can provide the same net electrochemical driving force, they perturb ion transport differently: voltage modifies transition rates throughout the permeation pathway, whereas chemical potential primarily alters ion uptake probabilities. Consequently, uptake, transfer, and release respond differently to the two driving forces, producing distinct flux signatures and causing chemical potential-driven flux to plateau while voltage-driven flux continues to increase. These differences encode the rate-limiting step (RLS) in open-channel flux. We propose a protocol based on three standard I-V measurements obtained under symmetric and asymmetric ion concentrations for elucidating the RLS. Application of this analysis to experimental data from the KcsA potassium channel identifies release as the RLS for outward permeation, consistent with available structural and computational evidence. Together, these results reveal how the physics of the electrochemical driving force shapes ion transport and provide an experimentally accessible strategy for connecting macroscopic electrophysiology measurements to microscopic transport mechanisms. One of the main challenges in the field of electrophysiology is connecting experimental currents from I-V data of ion channels to a detailed, atomistic mechanism of ion transport. We discovered that by examining the how the channel flux changes under different driving forces, we can identify the rate-, voltage-, and flux-limiting steps of ion transport. Understanding the relationships between ionic driving force and the corresponding channel behavior allows us to elucidate key details of the transport mechanism from macroscopic electrophysiology measurements.

papers.title: Comparison of Commercial Fixed and In-House Tissue-Based and Live Cell-Based Assays for the Detection of Common Neuronal Surface Autoantibodies.
papers.abstract: Autoimmune encephalitis (AIE) is diagnosed through detection of neuronal-surface antibodies (Abs) in serum and/or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Commercial biochip-based cell-based assay (CBA) using fixed cells and in-house CBAs using live cells may give incongruent results. We aimed to shed further light on features of AIE patients with discordant CBA results to establish factors related with diagnosis and treatment-response. A total of 45 patients found positive for N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR), leucine rich glioma inactivated 1 (LGI1), contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2)-Abs on routine screening done with fixed-CBA, were further tested using in-house live-CBA and tissue-based assay (TBA). Serum neurofilament light chain (NFL) levels were measured and response to immunotherapy was assessed in a follow-up period of 36.9±7.8 months. Thirty patients who were positive on both fixed and live-CBA/TBA, showed trends towards displaying limbic symptoms and EEG/MRI features suggestive of AIE. By contrast, most of the 15 patients with only fixed-CBA positivity failed to fulfill AIE criteria. Positivity on live CBA/TBA did not predict response to immunotherapy or coexisting cancers. Some patients in the fixed-CBA positive category exhibited features highly suggestive of autoimmune encephalopathy and elevated NFL levels. Lower disease severity, presence of viral prodromal findings, absence of autonomic symptoms and facial dyskinesia were associated with treatment response. Live CBA/TBA demonstrated higher diagnostic accuracy than fixed cell-based assays and substantially reduced the likelihood of false-positive antibody detection. Positive live-CBA/TBA results strongly coincide with definite AIE criteria. However, live CBA and NFL results fail to predict response to immunotherapy and identify coexisting cancers. This is putatively because some patients in the live-CBA/TBA negative category likely have immunotherapy-responsive neuroinflammatory disorders.

papers.title: A subtype-specific gene regulatory program controls differential circuit integration of deep CA3 pyramidal neurons
papers.abstract: How closely related neuronal subtypes integrate into different circuits remains poorly understood. Deep and superficial hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons (PNs) differ in intrinsic firing and mossy fiber (MF) input at specialized postsynaptic structures termed thorny excrescences (TEs). Combining developmental single-nucleus multiomics with genetic targeting, morphological analysis and electrophysiology, we identify the transcription factor ST18 as a regulator of deep CA3 subtype identity. ST18 marks sparsely thorny and burst-firing neurons, and gene regulatory analyses predict that it represses a superficial-associated program involved in dendritic spine development, synaptic organization, and electrophysiological properties. Postnatal ST18 loss shifts the transcriptional and chromatin landscape of deep CA3 PNs toward a superficial-like state. These molecular changes are accompanied by increased TE elaboration approaching superficial levels, enhanced excitatory synaptic activity, and reduced burst-firing. Together, these findings identify ST18-dependent restriction of an alternative subtype program as a mechanism linking molecular identity to distinct input connectivity patterns and intrinsic firing properties during postnatal circuit maturation.

papers.title: Excitation-contraction coupling plasticity is revealed upon RyR2 depletion in adult mouse ventricular myocytes.
papers.abstract: Ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is central to cardiac excitation-contraction coupling (ECC), translating electrical signals into sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca 2+ release and mechanical contraction. Although constitutive deletion of RyR2 is lethal, adult hearts can withstand a significant reduction in RyR2 expression without overt ECC dysfunction. We hypothesized that ECC possesses intrinsic homeostatic plasticity that rapidly adapts to acute RyR2 loss to maintain cardiac performance. Using an adult tamoxifen-inducible RyR2 conditional knockout (RyR2cKO) mouse model, we evaluated cardiac structure, electrophysiology, and intracellular Ca 2+ dynamics. RyR2cKO mice survived for weeks with <10% residual RyR2 protein expression. In vivo echocardiography and electrocardiography revealed normal cardiac structure and function. Confocal Ca 2+ imaging in intact hearts and isolated ventricular myocytes showed preserved Ca 2+ transient (CaT) amplitude but slower release kinetics and elevated SR load. Simultaneous patch-clamp and confocal Ca 2+ imaging established that L-type Ca 2+ current ( I Ca ) and ECC gain were maintained in RyR2cKO myocytes. Expression of Ca V 1.2, NCX, and phospholamban remained unchanged, whereas SERCA2a, IP 3 receptor, and VMP1 levels decreased. Pharmacological inhibition of IP 3 receptors did not suppress CaT, ruling out alternative SR channel compensation. These findings reveal remarkable intrinsic ECC plasticity, where high RyR2 channel reserve, elevated SR Ca 2+ load, and CaT autoregulation collectively maintain cardiac Ca 2+ cycling and contractile function despite profound RyR2 depletion. Deletion of RyR2, a critical channel for cardiac excitation-contraction coupling (ECC), is embryonically lethal; however, adult cardiomyocytes can tolerate a significant reduction in RyR2 expression without overt dysfunction. We show that mouse hearts and cardiomyocytes with a 90% reduction in RyR2 expression show preserved Ca 2+ handling. Compensation for reduced RyR2 levels does not involve overt remodeling of the ECC machinery or cardiac structure.Cardiomyocytes have a RyR2 reserve and employ autoregulation to maintain ECC fidelity, uncovering homeostatic plasticity as a regulatory mechanism of ECC.Reduced RyR2 expression is often observed in heart disease; however, it may not contribute to the pathology.

papers.title: 5-HT1A Antagonist WAY-100635 Prevents Chronic Neurodegeneration and Immune Activation After TBI.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) initiates secondary neurodegeneration that compromises interconnected neural circuits and contributes to persistent visual and neurobehavioral impairment. Pharmacological strategies that preserve vulnerable neurons and synapses while limiting chronic neuroinflammation remain an unmet therapeutic need. We previously identified the serotonin 1A receptor (5-HT1A) antagonist WAY-100635 through screening human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and demonstrated that it promotes neuroprotection through cyclic adenosine monophosphate-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis. Here, we investigated whether post-injury treatment extends this neuroprotective efficacy to cerebral and visual circuitry following TBI. Male C57BL/6J mice aged 2-3 months underwent unilateral controlled cortical impact (CCI) involving the left visual cortex. Mice were randomly assigned to sham, untreated injury or treated injury groups, with 3-10 sham controls and 5-8 mice per injury group across experiments. WAY-100635 was administered intraperitoneally at 5 mg/kg daily, beginning 1 hour after injury and continuing for 6 weeks. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed using motor and psychological-health-relevant risk-taking/behavioral disinhibition by elevated-plus-maze assessment, visual electrophysiology, optokinetic responses, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging, and retinal and cortical histopathology. Unilateral cortical injury produced bilateral RGC dysfunction and loss, with greater degeneration in the eye contralateral to the injured hemisphere, consistent with predominantly crossed murine visual projections. WAY-100635 significantly preserved RGC survival and function, improved visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and preserved visually evoked cortical responses to contralateral eye stimulation. Diffusion MRI revealed bilateral visual pathway abnormalities, with treatment selectively normalizing fractional anisotropy and radial kurtosis in the optic tract ipsilateral to cortical injury. In perilesional cortex, treatment preserved neuronal cell bodies and synapses detected by synaptophysin immunoreactivity while markedly reducing microglial/macrophage activation and reactive astrogliosis. These effects were accompanied by improved early motor performance and attenuation of injury-associated increases in open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze. Cortical cavity volume was not significantly reduced, supporting preferential protection of vulnerable circuitry surrounding and connected to the primary lesion. These findings identify post-injury WAY-100635 treatment as a novel therapeutic intervention that combines neuronal and synaptic preservation with reduced chronic glial activation and improved functional outcomes. They support further translational development of serotonin 1A receptor antagonism to limit secondary neurodegeneration and the visual and neurobehavioral consequences of TBI.

papers.title: Cardiac electrophysiology procedures must be performed exclusively by trained electrophysiologists: A statement from the Heart Rhythm Society and Heart Rhythm Advocates.
papers.abstract: The exponential growth of clinical cardiac electrophysiology (CCEP) as a subspecialty has created an important unresolved question in contemporary cardiovascular medicine: Who is qualified to perform electrophysiology (EP) procedures? As nonelectrophysiologists increasingly perform procedures that require the nuanced expertise of a trained or board-certified CCEP (eg, permanent pacemaker implantation, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation, cardiac resynchronization therapy, and transvenous lead extraction), the consequences for patient safety, procedural outcomes, and health system efficiency have become impossible to ignore. This article presents a comprehensive, evidence-based argument that cardiac EP procedures must be performed exclusively by physicians who have completed accredited fellowship training in CCEP. We draw upon peer-reviewed outcome data, guideline-derived training standards from the Heart Rhythm Society, the American College of Cardiology, and American Heart Association, including the newly published 2026 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Rhythm Society Advanced Training Statement on Clinical Cardiac Electrophysiology, as well as registry analyses spanning hundreds of thousands of patients to substantiate our position. The risks associated with suboptimal operator training are not theoretical; they are measurable, costly, and potentially fatal. The evidence presented demonstrates that operator specialization in EP is among the most powerful independent predictors of procedural safety and long-term outcomes and can be as important as institutional volume in many analyses. We call upon hospital credentialing committees, national medical societies, payers, regulatory bodies, and policymakers worldwide to establish and enforce a definitive standard: only trained CCEPs should implant and manage cardiac implantable electronic devices, perform catheter ablation procedures, execute transvenous lead extraction, and conduct formal EP studies.

papers.title: The ligament of Marshall as a therapeutic target in atrial fibrillation: from anatomy to catheter-based and surgical management-a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Long regarded as an inconsequential embryological remnant, the ligament of Marshall (LOM) is now recognized as a treatable component of the atrial fibrillation (AF) substrate. This review synthesizes the anatomical, electrophysiological and clinical evidence behind that shift and compares the two routes to the LOM: percutaneous retrograde ethanol infusion into the vein of Marshall (EIVOM) during catheter ablation, and direct division during thoracoscopic surgery. Both act on the same epicardial structure; only the route of access differs. A structured literature search of PubMed, Embase and Web of Science covered the embryology, anatomy, histology and electrophysiology of the LOM and clinical studies of both routes. Two authors screened and selected records independently. Given the heterogeneity of study designs, findings were synthesized narratively. The LOM is a neuro-muscular remnant of the embryonic left superior vena cava that contributes to AF through three mechanisms: triggers arising from insulated myocardial "Marshall bundles", autonomic modulation via adjacent ganglionated plexi, and preferential conduction across the mitral isthmus. Five randomized trials of EIVOM-based strategies have enrolled more than 1,100 patients; pooled analysis shows improved 12-month freedom from any atrial arrhythmia (risk ratio 1.16, 95% confidence interval: 1.04-1.29; number needed to treat 10) and less repeat ablation, without excess major complications (2.5% vs. 2.8%) but with more overall complications and longer fluoroscopy. Crucially, no trial has tested ethanol infusion in isolation; the observed benefit reflects composite lesion sets. Thoracoscopic division interrupts the entire ligament independent of venous anatomy but has never been a randomized variable; randomized evidence for thoracoscopic and hybrid strategies overall ranges from neutral (CASA-AF) to positive (CONVERGE, HARTCAP-AF). Guidelines recognize both as options in selected patients without mandating routine LOM division. The LOM is a reproducible, anatomically defined target reachable percutaneously or by surgical division within a comprehensive AF ablation strategy. The supporting evidence is markedly asymmetric: randomized data exist for EIVOM-based strategies but never for ethanol infusion alone, none at all for surgical division, and the two routes have never been compared head-to-head. Its incremental benefit beyond pulmonary vein and posterior wall isolation remains undefined.
